Rivian Automotive — The electric vehicle maker jumped over 8% after it reported better-than-expected third-quarter results. Rivian lost an adjusted 48 cents per share on revenue of $2.16 billion. Amazon —Shares slipped nearly 6% in the premarket after the e-commerce giant reported third-quarter results that missed analyst expectations. The company also posted negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion . Reddit — The company announced it will require users create official accounts to access its social media platform and issued weaker-than-expected revenue guidance for the fourth quarter. Shares tumbled 21%. Crypto-related stocks — Bitcoin, Coinbase and Robinhood stocks shed over 4% following one of the largest crypto hacks ever on Thursday when Binance reported an estimated $6.3 billion was impacted. The company also estimates roughly $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets were frozen. Chevron — The energy company gained 1.4% after reporting its net income surged nearly 200% to $9.9 billion in the third quarter. Chevron also posted better-than-expected revenue for the period. Exxon Mobil — Shares gained more than 1.4% after the oil giant's profits doubled to $15.4 billion from $7.5 billion in the year-earlier period. AstraZeneca — Shares for the biopharmaceutical company jumped over 5% following better-than-expected third-quarter earnings. Fallon | Afp | Getty Images Chevron and ExxonMobil on Friday reported profits that surged in the third quarter, as their U.S. refineries ran at full capacity to take advantage of high diesel fuel prices. Chevron's net income surged nearly 200% to $9.9 billion, or $5.06 a share, compared to $3.5 billion, or $1.82 a share, in the same period last year. When adjusted for one-time items, it reported earnings of $5.28 per share, soundly beating Wall Street's expectations of $4.89. Diesel prices have surged globally as Ukraine and Iran have bombed refineries in Russia and the Middle East. U.S. refiners have ramped up production to fill the supply gap. ExxonMobil's profits doubled to $15.4 billion, or $3.72 a share, compared to $7.5 billion, or $1.76 a share, in the same period in 2025. When adjusted for one-time items, it posted earnings of $4.23 a share, beating the Street's expectations. Chevron shares are up about 2% in premarket trading, while Exxon is trading about 1.5% higher. Here's how Chevron and Exxon did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG: Chevron's earnings per share: $5.28 adjusted, vs. $4.89 expected Chevron's revenue: $67.8 billion, vs. $61.6 billion expected Exxon's earnings per share: $4.23 adjusted, vs. $4.08 expected Exxon's revenue: $113.2 billion, vs. $103.1 billion expected Chevron's U.S. refineries processed record amounts of crude oil at just above 1 million barrels per day, as the facilities ran at 98% capacity. Diesel and jet fuel yields rose more than 10%, the company said. Exxon's Gulf Coast refineries operated at 100% utilization with the second-highest diesel production on record at those facilities, the company said. Profits from Chevron's refining division surged more than 300% to $4.9 billion compared to $1.1 billion in the same period in 2025. Its oil and gas production generated earnings of $5.7 billion, up 70% from $3.3 billion in the year-ago period. Exxon's refining division generated profits of about $7.2 billion in the quarter, outpacing its production business' earnings of about $7.1 billion. Its refining profits have surged nearly 200% to $11.4 billion so far this year compared to $4 billion during the first nine months of 2025. Chevron's output actually declined slightly to 3.9 million barrels per day compared to about 4 million bpd in the same period last year. The decline was in its international segment due in part to the conflict in the Middle East, while output was largely flat in the U.S. year over year. Exxon has produced about 4.5 million bpd this year, a more than 2% decline from nearly 4.7 million during the first nine months of 2025. headlines.article_text: Trump tech allies swap AI for 'super intelligence' in earnings calls Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX adopted President Trump's preferred "super intelligence" term on their third-quarter earnings calls. Last month, Trump ordered that the term super intelligence replace artificial intelligence within the government. The CEOs of Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet stuck with AI on their earnings calls this week In this article META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT US President Donald Trump speaks with Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg at the White House driveway following a luncheon for tech leaders in the East Room, in Washington, D.C., US, Sept. 29, 2026. Kevin Lamarque | Reuters A month after President Donald Trump ordered that the term "super intelligence" replace artificial intelligence within executive branch departments and agencies, his leading tech allies — Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg — followed suit on earnings calls. Their fellow tech CEOs were less eager to do the same. Trump's declaration took place on Sept. 29, while he was hosting an AI luncheon at the White House for industry leaders. At the time, he was working to ensure the growth of AI in the U.S. with limited regulations. The president this week announced on Truth Social that he's banning the use of AI or artificial intelligence in "all relevant documents" and "everything else." SpaceX and Tesla adhered to Trump's wishes on earnings calls last week after Musk, earlier in October, changed the name of his rocket company's AI division to SpaceXSI. Speaking on Tesla's call about his work on humanoid robots, Musk said, "Some of them look very impressive, but they're not really using any kind of advanced AI or SI." Zuckerberg was equally compliant on Meta's earnings call on Oct. 21, emphasizing his company's "goal of delivering personal superintelligence to everyone." However, Meta was already using the term, having created a unit called Meta Superintelligence Labs last year. While Musk and Zuckerberg have been perhaps the fiercest supporters of the Trump administration among tech's CEOs, they're by no means outliers. Leaders of all the tech giants have contributed to Trump's inauguration festivities or his plan for the White House ballroom , and some have been intentional about getting rid of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs that the president opposed. But for now at least, they're holding out when it comes to eliminating the term AI. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy peppered his call with use of AI on Thursday , uttering the acronym well over a dozen times in his introductory remarks. A day earlier, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said one of the company's three points of focus is "designing AI to empower people." And Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai was seconds into his quarterly earnings commentary when he said the search giant's "AI investments are driving increased usage and overall user growth." Trump's attempted rebrand comes just ahead of the midterm elections next week, with the Republican Party in jeopardy of losing control of both the House and Senate. Trump's job approval has been dropping and his economic approval rating just hit an all-time low, according to the latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey released last week. 'Real-world outcomes' That's not to suggest tech execs sticking with "AI" on this week's earnings calls are openly defying the president. Trump's preferred term is seeping into other correspondence and documents. Microsoft's annual report filed last week included eight mentions of super intelligence, starting at the top of the letter to shareholders. "For Microsoft, the central question as we enter this Super Intelligence era is not just how big the opportunity becomes, but how we deliver the real-world outcomes that every country, community, and company demands and deserves," Nadella wrote.
